newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian govt wants Telstra float in 1997.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian govt wants Telstra float in 1997.

text.p: Australian Finance Minister John Fahey said on Thursday he wanted the proposed public share offer of its wholly-owned telecommunications carrier Telstra Corp to occur in calendar 1997.
"I want it ready to go to the market this year, this calendar year," Fahey told reporters.
"But I am not saying it will," he said.
Fahey also announced the brokers for the planned float which is estimated to raise a minimum of A$8.0 billion.

"If it is appropriate to go to the market this year, we are ready to go to the market this year," Fahey said. He added if was difficult to tell what the share market conditions would be for the rest of the year.
Fahey said the float would not be underwritten in Australia, where 65 percent of the offer is to be sold, but the shares offered in the United States would be underwritten.

"Will the offer be underwritten? not in Australia, but legal requirements in the United States do require underwriting," he said. Two percent of the offer is set aside for Telstra employees and foreign investors are entitled to 35 percent.
Fahey would not comment on how much the government expects to raise from the partial privatisation of Telstra. "I want to get optimum value for taxpayers of Australia," Fahey said.

He would not comment either on the float structure, but added the government still had to consider the redeemable preference share issue option that was proposed by Independent Australian senator Brian Harridine.
The government is currently reviewing the redeemable share issue and expects to release the results of the review by the end of March, he said.

Fahey said the government would consider an instalment receipts share offer as part of the Telstra share offer structure. Instalment receipts were used in the government's sale of its remaining stake in the Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA) last year.
"We can't rule it out," Fahey said. "It was an attractive approach," he said.
He said the government would be able to terminate the agreement with any broking firm involved in the Telstra float if there was a conflict of interest.

"They will not be able to take part in other transactions which the Commonwealth (government) considers to be a conflict of interest and that includes taking part in a public offer of some other telecommunications group," Fahey said.
Telstra's rival Optus Communications Pty Ltd plans a share market float this year.
